You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test `StringUtilsTest.testEqualsCS1()` exercises the `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)` method. This method first handles null and identity checks and special-cases when both sequences are Strings. Otherwise, it calls `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` with these arguments: the two CharSequences, case sensitivity flag false, start indices 0, and the length equal to the max length of the two sequences.

The bug report indicates that `equals` can fail with a String Index Out of Bounds Exception (OBE) if the two sequences have different lengths.

Inspecting `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(CharSequence, boolean, int, CharSequence, int, int)` reveals the root cause: it attempts to compare the specified length (passed from equals as the max length of the two sequences) character-by-character. It iterates up to `length` but uses the indices to access characters in both sequences.

When the length is the max length, and sequences differ in length, `charAt(index)` will go beyond the shorter sequence's range, causing an index OBE.

Thus, the `equals` method calls `regionMatches` asking it to compare beyond the length of the shorter CharSequence. The `regionMatches` function does not check that the available length in both sequences is sufficient before indexing; it just blindly assumes the given length can be accessed safely.

The failing test cases exercising `equals` with different length sequences (e.g., new StringBuilder("abc") vs new StringBuilder("abcd")) trigger this issue because `regionMatches` attempts to read past the end of the shorter `CharSequence`.

This diagnosis aligns perfectly with the bug report's statement that the method fails with String Index OBE when lengths differ.

The fix should involve changing `StringUtils.equals` so it calls `regionMatches` with the length equal to the minimum of the two sequences' lengths (not the maximum). This ensures `regionMatches` never accesses past the end of either sequence.

In summary:
- `StringUtils.equals` calls `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` passing max length of sequences as length to compare.
- `regionMatches` accesses characters up to that length without bounds checking.
- If sequences have different lengths, `regionMatches` tries to read past the shorter one, causing String Index OBE.
- The failing test case demonstrates this with two different length StringBuilders.
- Changing equals to pass the minimum length would prevent the out-of-bounds access.

Recent bug reports don't seem relevant to this core indexing issue and mainly discuss other unrelated topics like null handling or constant visibility.

Therefore, the defect is localized to the `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)` method's usage of `regionMatches` length argument and can be fixed by revising the length argument passed.

Suggested fix location:
- `org.apache.commons.codec.binary.StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)`

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
